utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, here in tab 624 you gave a list of commanders -- sorry, a list of VJ members who were killed in the area of responsibility of the 549th Motorised Brigade in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, ending with number 31, is a list of our soldiers, members of the army, who were killed before the start of NATO aggression. Starting with number 32 until 230 are members of the VJ who were killed during the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A certain number of soldiers or, rather, the overwhelming majority of soldiers were killed in combat with terrorist forces, and a number of them were killed as a result of NATO airstrikes. So these two causes of death, basically combat with terrorists and NATO airstrikes, account for the death of all these soldiers. In view of this very large number, 200 soldiers killed during the aggression by the NATO alliance, most of them killed by Siptar terrorist forces, what would you say this evidence shows?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This evidence or, rather, this fact that 230 soldiers were killed in the zone of responsibility that covers primarily the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and the border belt with Albania, speaks to the intensity of the fighting with terrorist forces in 1998 and especially in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could the conclusion be drawn from this in any way that those people killed were killed by the army in various places?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, did any of these soldiers get killed by civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they couldn't have been killed by civilians. All of them were killed by terrorists or by bombs or NATO action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At the same time in 625, you provide a list of MUP members of the Republic of Serbia who were killed in the zone of responsibility of the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are policemen who were killed also in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a number -- up to number 29 are those killed before the NATO aggression, and after number 29 are those killed during the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from 29 to 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of these policemen get killed by civilians or in combat with KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed either by mines laid by the KLA along roads and by NATO airstrikes, by the bombing. And in both categories you should add about three times more people who were wounded in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. I think this suffices. I would now like to move on to 626, which you already referred to on an earlier occasion. What does this document contain? It is entitled "A survey of criminal proceedings initiated against perpetrators of criminal offences in the zone of the 549th Motorised Brigade in May 1998 to July 1999." Could you give us your briefest comment.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a total of 132 items. Most of these people are members of my units, but a certain number are terrorists, members of the KLA who were caught on the border, disarmed, and in 1998 were sent to the military court and in 1999 were sent to the war court. Under one of these columns you can see which -- with which crimes they were charged, and another column shows the verdicts, at least those that were known at the time of -- when this document was developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Nice pointed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that in English? Where are the verdicts that are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, it says "Decision of the Court." The one but last column. One but last.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Decisions of the court are indicated in those cases where they were made by the time the document was created. In other cases the indication says that the case is ongoing or that the case was referred to the competent court for the relevant territory. For instance, under item 39 we have a soldier charged with murder, sentenced to five years in prison. Then in number -- under number 103 we have another case. Mr. Nice says that officers were not prosecuted, but here under number 103 we have a major charged with war crime against civilian population, place of perpetration Prizren, sentenced to seven years in prison, and after appeal by the prosecutor, 14 years. Then three lines down there is a captain charged with war crime against civilian population, five years in prison, and that was changed to nine years after appeal by prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before you continue, let me just find the section of the indictment that deals with Article 7(3). Perhaps Mr. Kay or Mr. Nice -- on page 6, yes. Mr. Nice or Mr. Kay, are the acts or omissions of the subordinates referred to confined to the crimes that are charged in the indictment or are they referable to other crimes that were committed by those subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the way the indictment is framed, the indictment alleges specific counts against the accused, and this trial is based on those counts within the indictment. So the issues relating to those counts are those that are applied to the Article 7(3) issues, and that's what the Tribunal is specifically looking at in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because the evidence which the accused has been bringing in relation to this matter do not specifically relate to the counts, it appears to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. He's not been incident specific to the counts in the indictment, so what's being brought to the Court's attention are other incidents where there has been due process within the proceedings. One's got to remember this is 1999. The question was asked earlier as to, well, what happened further on? Well, of course, he was brought to this Tribunal in 2001, and the cases having been referred to a military court and on to a civilian court inevitably have a temporal factor involved, and one's got to consider that issue in relation to drawing any conclusions against this accused upon such -- such matters if cases are going through the appropriate procedures within the FRY jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the significance of this evidence is that it shows a culture of due process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was, contrary to the Prosecution allegations that this was a police state, that the defendant connived and created the conditions that were in existence at the time, that he actually had in place, constitutionally as well as factually, processes within the FRY system, and warnings having been given to citizens, those involved in public duty such as the army, the police, which he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They would not by themselves serve -- this evidence would not by itself serve to contradict the allegation of a breach of Article 7(3) in relation to the crimes charged, and in a sense it would be contradictory if Mr. Milosevic were to try to do that, because his case, as I understand it, is that he's not responsible for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's not responsible for those crimes and he's able to show that there were procedures in existence for dealing with those crimes. The issue of knew or ought to have known whether the acts of subordinates were such that they were committing crimes requires a balance and judgement as to what is exactly expected of a head of state. It's not an issue of negligence here and it's not an issue of absolute strict liability. If a crime is proven to have been committed, it can't be said that he has a 7(3) responsibility. What's got to be considered is what were the mechanisms in place and were these mechanisms applied to instances such as this. It would be far too high a standard to say that any crime that was committed, because of 7(3) responsibility, was something for which he was criminally liable. This is a matter that ultimately has to be judged to see what steps were taken and if they were reasonable and if he was in a position to have dealt with certain of the crimes that are alleged to have been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, can you find in that list that we're now looking at the case we looked at earlier, which was, I think, Topalovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't have a translation of this document. What has happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The details of this soldier, it has to do with Article 146 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is unlawful killing and wounding of the enemy. The place where the crime was perpetrated is Prizren and its surroundings, and the case was referred to the municipal prosecutor's office in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then would you say that on the information we had earlier there was a basis for describing the victim as the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The victim was a civilian. All of this was compiled by the official organs. So I'm reading what was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would he be described as the enemy in what you've just read to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that that's the way it has been written in this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the professional organs. Probably because this was considered to be a crime, a war crime where higher sentences are envisaged for the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand on what basis this person could be described as the enemy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, he's not described as the enemy. What is mentioned here is Article 146 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say unlawful killing and wounding of the enemy. That was the basis that was used to indict him for murder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that is an article that is valid in wartime, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What happens if you kill a friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a more serious qualification. The killing of a friend would be qualified as a killing, a murder, whereas Article 146 is a very grave crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, with all due apologies, due to the fact that my documents are incomplete, probably through some technical error, I have nothing in tab 623. When speaking of the NATO operations, could you please just say something about this map. Through the kindness of the liaison officer I have the map now. This is a map of locations bombed using depleted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. uranium in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you please explain this map in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, the first map is a NATO map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The one that's in English?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a NATO map. They submitted it, and it shows the regions where they used depleted uranium in their attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that map on the overhead projector now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on the overhead projector. It's up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this map in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please ask the technical people to show the map that's on the easel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a NATO map. It says "NATO K4, unclass."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map shows the territory that was targeted using cluster bombs, and especially those where depleted uranium was used. When looking at this map, we can see that part of Metohija just by the Albanian border was targeted very frequently, that is to say using large quantities of such ammunition. In other parts of Kosovo there is very little or, rather, considerably less. And then there is the area of Bujanovac and Presevo. In that area, Bujanovac-Presevo-Vranje, there were also attacks with depleted uranium. It was used 8/10s and seven barrel guns gatling were used for this depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, did you look at this using proper expertise, what this use of depleted uranium meant and the time required for the danger of radiation from this depleted uranium to be over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, first if he can explain the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again it goes to the fear factor, the general climate of what was covering this region at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so might be related to the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The forcible transfer, the migration of people. The conditions and climate created by NATO and the KLA, the manner of the bombardment, the weapons used, the missiles used, the fear that was engendered into the population caused them to migrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard my question, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me in the briefest possible terms what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody with at least a bit of knowledge in physics knows that depleted uranium, that is uranium 238, is highly radioactive, and 3.7 billion years is the time it takes to decompose. So practically it is limitless. It is very dangerous. If I can say a lethal dose or, rather, a person who takes a particle of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Frankly, I'm taken by surprise by so much of this material that another dose of expertise of this kind is perhaps neither here nor there but it is expert matter and I can't be expected to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, I think you have shown me up, because I didn't know that. What kind of background would you have that would enable you to give this kind of evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any officer knows this, I believe of any army in the world. As far as my army is concerned, with the training we've had, any officer who completed the military academy has to know about that, those who did not undergo additional training. It is simply ridiculous to say there is a lack of knowledge or, rather, that we would have a lack of knowledge of atomic weapons and their radioactivity. That is something that we learn at the military academy, as far as back as that. After all, this is something that is studied in physics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, tell us in the briefest possible terms what it is that you know. We have established that you have the right kind of education for answering this because you have completed the proper schools. You studied this, and you took tests in this field.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So tell us briefly what you know about this.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This territory of Kosovo and Metohija, which was targeted with depleted uranium, is practically polluted forever because 3.7 billion years is such a long period. Scientists probably cannot prove even that the earth has been that -- in existence for that long and will it continue to exist for another 4.7 billion years. So forever this territory will continue to be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not on the transcript. I was asking whether there were refugees in that area. What's the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that that population had left the area. It had fled. As for my army that was in that territory and, generally speaking, the army of Yugoslavia, there is already a number of professionals and soldiers who have died of leukaemia and cancer. Some died soon after the war, others are still being treated. Also among the reserve soldiers, there is a large number of those who are sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What quantity of uranium was dispersed through this area, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is where the thrust of the attack came, a total of 30 and 40 -- between 30 and 40 tons of uranium was thrown there. That is our estimate. My zone and the zone of the 125th Brigade was targeted most of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much depleted uranium does one particular charge contain, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... evidence now on this matter insofar as it is relevant. I rule we have had enough evidence. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The minefields in this map, are those mines the ones planted by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb army set up minefields only by the border. If there are some minefields depicted, they're along the border with Albania or facing the Republic of Macedonia. Those could be our minefields except that we gave KFOR total records for each and every one of these minefields. If we are looking at the territory in-depth, then these are mines and minefields that were placed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this include areas where cluster bombs were thrown that can also be considered to be mines?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. NATO probably depicted that too. They actually showed areas where they used cluster bombs. That is practically throughout the territory of the state but particularly in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are dispersed mines throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please explain very briefly the organisational structure of the army in war and peace, then the schematic pertaining to the army command and of the 3rd Army. We have all of that in tab 628 -- or, rather, 626. And the diagram of the Pristina Corps. In the briefest possible terms. And finally you have the diagram of your brigade. So you're a general, and you have the diagram of the structure from the top to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we start with the schematic of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia in peacetime, it is headed by the Chief of General Staff, who has his own office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we speed things up, because -- by putting it on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can have these on the overhead projector because they're not translated, unless the Court has got translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. We must have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab number should be 628, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, one by one could you explain these schematics briefly so we know what it's about. You have the army of Yugoslavia as a whole in wartime and in peacetime, then the command diagram in war and peacetime.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of General Staff, with his office and his deputy. Then the department for communications with foreign military representatives is there, and also the security department. Then also the sectors.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Milosevic and the general, if you look at the transcript, you'll see that the interpreters are asking you to slow down. Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you not to read out abbreviations but to say the entire wording. Don't say "Cov," for example, say "land forces."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's move on from the beginning. The sector for operational and staff activities. Then the sector for the army, the land forces. The sector for the air force and anti-aircraft defence. The sector for the navy. The sector for communications, electronic surveillance and reconnaissance. The sector for mobilisation and manning. The sector for training. The sector for logistics and the inspection of the army of Yugoslavia. And then we have the independent departments linked directly to the Chief of the General Staff, the department for information and moral guidance, information department, security department, and administration for housing, or department for housing. The sectors that I have mentioned have within their composition certain departments or administrations, depending on what the sector is. I don't think we need go into those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is the General Staff in peace. Now we come to the General Staff in wartime, the next one. So the Chief of the General Staff, the Deputy Chief of the General Staff. That part is the same as in peacetime. And then where we had the sector for operations and staff affairs, it has two administrations now and two departments. It is subdivided into those four. Instead of the sector for the land forces, we have the administration for the land forces. Instead of the sector for RV and PVO, or rather air defence, et cetera, we have the administration for air defence, the air force and air defence. Instead of the sector for the navy, we now have the administration for the navy. Then we also have the administration for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic defence systems; the administration for mobilisation, replenishment of cadres and systemic questions; the administration for information and moral guidance. We have the logistics sector that remains a sector. Then we have the administration for security and the inspection of the army of Yugoslavia. And directly linked to the administration of replenishment of cadres, mobilisation and systemic questions is the supreme military court and supreme military prosecutor, whereas for the sector for operations and staff affairs we have the centre for intelligence and surveillance linked to that one. And the administration security is linked or, rather, the counter-intelligence centre of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia is linked to the security administration. The other smaller departments I don't think we need go into at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the next page is the schematic for commanding the Yugoslav army in peacetime and in war once again.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These direct lines, or chains of command down the line, denote the chain of command and management and command. The interrupted line, dotted line, denotes coordination and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But could you put your pointer to the dotted line so we can see what that means, because on the overhead projector you can't really see this properly or clearly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This full line is the line of command and control. The interrupted line, the dotted line, shows the line of coordination and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we have the Supreme Defence Council at the top there, and if you go down the line, the uninterrupted arrow, the full line.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here, the Supreme Defence Council, then we have the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, and then this goes further, further down towards the units and the individual commands. That's the chain of command from top to bottom. Then we have the dotted line towards the federal government, the line of coordination and cooperation, and from the General Staff the dotted line going towards the Federal Ministry of Defence. Coordination and cooperation once again, that's the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now we have the schematic for wartime commanding.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take it from the top. Here we can see that chain of command: The Supreme Defence Council is at the top, the president of the FRY, with his military cabinet or officers to which we have the Guards Brigade linked, and then the Chief of the General Staff with their cabinets and deputies. Then we come to the sectors of administration, which we saw previously and explained, and directly for the Chief of the General Staff we have the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Armies linked to him, the air defence systems and air force, the navy and the three smaller units; the 46th Motorised Brigade, the 72nd Special Brigade, and the Anti-terrorist Brigade, detachment. Kobra is its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, since this is very important for the chain of command, could you show us the levels of command of the army of Yugoslavia, that schematic, which is the next schematic that we come to, the next diagram. We have groups here, groupings, and when you go down to the concrete specific units, we have six levels of command down that chain, lower down.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have the Supreme Defence Council at the top once again. That is the supreme organ, the supreme body and supreme level of command, the top-most level. Then we have the president who is the -- presides over the supreme council of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then those squares or -- we have the President of the FRY there, and to him we have the General Staff linked, and then after the General Staff, what are the levels? Could you show this, could you indicate this to us on the overhead projector. We can't see it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Linked to the General Staff, we have the armies, the army level: Three armies, the air force and anti-air defence, and the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So underneath the armies, we have the corps.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then we come to the brigades and regiments.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the division, one division there. The division level is the first level, then the second level is the brigades level, then the third level is the battalion level, then the fourth level is the company level or battery level. Level five is the platoon level, and level six is [indiscernible] level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, General. That's that one. Now, let's take a specific example. The 3rd Army, for example, which the Pristina Corps came under, and your brigade specifically. Let's take a look at what that was like. I'd like to look at the schematic for the 3rd Army structure in wartime to save time. Not to go through the peacetime one but through the war diagram.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is the organisational structure the 3rd Army in wartime. The commander of the 3rd Army is at the top there, and then that is his command, and it is composed of a staff and headquarters. Do you want me to go down the line there, what the staff comprises of and the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, you needn't go into those details.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we come to the box next door. It is the department for information and psychological and propaganda effects, the security department, the legal department, the personnel department, and the logistics department, and then linked to the commander directly we have two corps linked to him the Nis Corps and the Pristina Corps. Then once again the individual units at lower level linked to the army command. The Nis Corps has its brigades and regiments. Do you want me to go through that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No need. Let's look at the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps has its own units there and they are the independent units within the composition of the 3rd Army, which means that we're now going down the Pristina -- the Pristina Corps. The commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have the direct link of the brigades linked to the commander. Let's go further down. The 78th Brigade, for example, and lower down we have its battalions, so I won't mention them, just the brigades. The 78th Brigade, the 125th Brigade, the 549th Brigade, the 354th, the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade, the 159th Artillery Brigade, PVO, the 15th Armoured Brigade, the 243rd Mechanised Brigade, and the 352nd Engineers Regiment. And the corps had independent battalions as well: The 52nd Battalion for special purposes, the 52nd Battalion for communications, the 54 for the medical corps, the 54 Battalion of the BHO, the 52nd Additional Battalion, and the 49th Pontoon Company, and some other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, we've seen where the brigades come in. Now look at the 549th Motorised Brigade of yours in wartime; the commander and then down the line, down the chain.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my 549th Motorised Brigade. I am the commander in that one. I have my staff, I have assistant commander for moral guidance, I have the organ for security and the organ for logistics. They are directly linked to me. Then we have directly linked to me three motorised battalions; the armoured battalion, the howitzer artillery battalion 122 millimetres, mixed anti-armoured artillery battalion, a light artillery battalion PVO, and Engineers Battalion or company. And then we have the subordinated units: The 40 Bofors millimetre unit, the Prizren unit with the 108th and 68th Detachment, the 354th Detachment, the 55th Border Battalion, the 3rd company from the 53rd Border Battalion, two batteries 128 millimetres, they are called Oganj, and one battery 155 millimetres from the corps artillery brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you for those explanations. Now would you go back for a moment to the schematic of the level of command of the army of Yugoslavia that we had previously, the command level where we can see the chain of command from the Supreme Defence Council, the president of the FRY, and the General Staff, the level of the armies, the corps level, the division level, brigades, battalions, companies, batteries, squads, et cetera. Now, my question to you is this: At any point in time -- and this is also the chain of command, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time was the chain of command disrupted in that one and a half years about which you are testifying?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chain of command was never interrupted or disrupted in any way. It always had three levels; strategic, strategic operative, and tactical, those three levels. The strategic level is that one, the strategic operations level at the level of the army and the corps, whereas the other six levels down the line are tactical levels; divisions, brigades, battalions, companies, regiments and squads, and the chain of command always went down that chain. That was the chain, those were the links towards the subordinate units or, rather, reporting from the ground roots level, subordinate level, up to the command level, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the second tactical level of command is where you were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the tactical level is the second tactical level, just after the division level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Fine. Now, since you have just the corps above you in your specific situation, you were, practically speaking, at the first level of tactical command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between us and the corps, that was the direct link, the direct chain line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Fine. Now, you had from top to bottom and from bottom to top reporting and communication throughout that chain of command. During those -- that communication, did you have any orders, or coming down from your subordinates levels did you have any reports coming from top to bottom or from bottom to top about -- reports about any specific order or any kind of decision which can be tied up with any kind of war crime? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now let's move on. Just a few more questions. You have explained to us all the movements of units, what you did throughout the material time. Now, what was the relationship between the members of the army of Yugoslavia towards civilians and Albanian civilians? What was their attitude?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking in general terms, globally, that attitude and relationship can be termed to be proper, correct, and professional, with exceptional -- with exceptions as individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The individual cases that we mentioned, for the ones you learned about, was -- were they sanctioned in keeping with the law?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Regardless of how we reached information, through which chain of command, security chain, or other state organs, each individual case was dealt with. Precisely because of the morale of the unit and combat readiness of the unit, it was sanctioned forthwith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. You said that the attitude of the members of the army towards Albanian civilians was professional, did you not? Proper and correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, can we take a look at the DVD that we have and can we see some of that on the footage?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As there are quite a number of DVDs, a lot of footage, we've already seen some of those excerpts. We saw the army. We saw soldiers and -- and their relationship with other state organs and civilians, how they dealt with the problem of bombing, of the bombardment. We saw that, and we have more footage of that kind. We also have footage from the surrounding area of Djakovica, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Djakovica and a DVD interviewing some Albanians, and that's the next one.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Prizren and Prizren Has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw this one, the 14th of May. May we see the next clip. We saw this one yesterday. Let's go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another village, called Zjum, near Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is from May 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is this place called Prizren Has, and Zjum village is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us see this one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned at one point, General, a village called Osik near Djakovica. That is the subject of the next video clip, tab 629. 479 is the one we've just seen. Let us see the last one, and then we'll move on to the last few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Nice is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suppose a point arises about the admissibility of this kind of material. We have plenty of films of records of the conflict in Yugoslavia and they're typically not admitted. We have, the Prosecution, The Death of Yugoslavia as an example. Sometimes passages have been where there is a particular reason to admit them. Thus far, over our objections, documents have been admitted which have in some way been connected to the witness producing them, as in the case of Lituchy. He says he conducted the interviews himself, or in Andric he was present when they were conducted, things like that. I'm not sure that this witness has actually provided any particularly good reason why the Chamber should depart from its exception and admit this kind of material, but it's matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness. General, tell us about the source of this film that we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was filmed by the state television, Radio-Television of Serbia, the Prizren studio. The editor of that studio is Boris Ugrinovic, and the cameraman, as I said yesterday -- I said yesterday who the cameraman was. His name was Sanjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have another clip that is directly relevant to the army. It says "Albanians, Turks and the Roma in the army --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will wait until the Chamber has considered this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit the video -- or the film, rather. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This clip is entitled "Albanians, Turks, and the Roma in the Yugoslav army in April 1999." Can we see it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do we have another clip, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you have another one, I think that will have to -- that will have to be shown after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you now at the end of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I just have a few more questions related to certain counts in the indictment. Just a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, remember, no leading questions. And I do not want your usual tactic of asking questions in relation to the indictment that are properly the province of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot underestimate the witness by asking him leading questions. If something sounds leading to you, that is certainly not my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Many of the questions that you ask are, in my view, provocatively leading. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, we left off at this last video clip where we saw Albanians, Turks, and the Roma in the ranks of the army of Yugoslavia. Could you tell me very briefly, in the units over which you had command, were there any Albanians, Turks, and the Roma?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Members of all ethnic communities were represented in the units. As far as Albanians are concerned, in combat units we had primarily Albanians who were natives of the entire Serbia, especially the southern part of Serbia around Bujenovac and Presevo. The greatest part of Albanians from Kosovo were not in the regular army. The men we saw were in the so-called military territorial unit because all the other Albanians, citizens of Serbia, were military conscripts and were on military records. Thus I had, for instance, a unit composed entirely of Turks. And there was a platoon commanded by a major, a Turk. I had a unit of 1.200 people manned by the Gorani, Muslims. They had their own commanders of the same ethnicity. Then I had another unit with only one Serb in it, and all the others, there were reservists, were Muslims from the area of Sredecka Zupa [phoen]. So you could say in my unit I had a lot of Hungarians, Slovaks. I think 70 per cent of men were Serbs and others were members of other ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that generally reflects the proportions of various ethnic groups in Serbia, doesn't it? Thank you, General. We've gone through 1998 and 1999 by various incidents that happened in those years, and now I would like to tell you what is written in paragraph 53 of the indictment, which relates to Kosovo. Of course there are other people mentioned, but it says: "... beginning on or about the 1st of January, 1999, and continuing until 20th of June, 1999, he ... planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at Kosovo Albanian civilians living in Kosovo in the FRY. "Carried out by forces of the FRY and Serbia targeting Kosovo Albanians with the objective of expelling a substantial portion of the Kosovo Albanian population from Kosovo in an effort to ensure continued Serbian control over the province." This was a quotation from the indictment. We looked at various levels of command and we located your particular level of command. That is the first out of six levels. So in view of your constant presence in Kosovo and your position that you occupied there, could this allegation be corroborated by any fact that is known to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is exactly what I said you are not to do. You have read to him substantially two paragraphs of the indictment and you're asking him whether that's correct. Ultimately, we'll decide that on the basis of the evidence. You have led evidence from him which relates to these matters, and we'll make a determination on the basis of the evidence. You don't take the matter any further by asking the witness to offer a conclusion on these paragraphs of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. Robinson. In this paragraph it says that the forces of the FRY, and those are the forces that General Delic commanded within his area of responsibility, that they undertook a widespread campaign or systematic campaign of terror and violence. I'm putting a perfectly neutral question: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question you're putting to him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quoted all this about the widespread campaign of terror and violence and the objective why this was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in that territory all the time. My area of responsibility was very wide. It covered a very wide territory. Such cases or such conduct by the security forces - I'm referring to the forces of the Ministry of the Interior and of the army - there is nothing that can be brought into this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 55, it says that: "The forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo." And they "... intentionally created an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force, and acts of violence." General, did the army expel Albanians, as is said here?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These days we showed quite a few documents and now, to put in the briefest possible terms, the army protected the entire population of Kosovo and Metohija regardless of whether they were Serbs or Albanians. As for the departure of the population to Albania, there are other sources which were not all mentioned here either. I can also say that the departure of the population to Albania is part of a broader campaign against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, have you ever heard of any plan of violence or of expulsion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I had different plans in my hands, but they were all plans of defending our own country, or parts of the territory of our country or of Kosovo and Metohija where I was commander. Absolutely never, except for when I listened to the charges here and the indictment here during the testimony of various witnesses, did I hear of such a plan. So such a plan never existed in the army and in the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 56, it says: "Throughout Kosovo, forces of the FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians. This was accomplished by the widespread shelling of towns and villages; the burning and destruction of property, including homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments and religious sites; and the destruction of personal property." Please, did the army do that, or the security forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that at that time in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and after that there were many damaged buildings that belonged to all ethnic communities. Throughout Kosovo and Metohija there was fighting against terrorists, and in this fighting there were some facilities that were destroyed. Some facilities were damaged or destroyed apart from combat, but they were investigated, especially by the Ministry of the Interior. The army absolutely did not take part in any kind of intentional destruction of facilities, deliberate destruction, or creating unbearable living conditions for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is also claimed in the same paragraph that the forces of the army of Yugoslavia escorted expelled Kosovo Albanians to the borders, thus trying to keep them under control, and their movement under control too, that they came on foot and on -- in columns of thousands of people, tractors, buses, trailers and trucks, as well as on trains, buses or trucks which were organised and provided by forces of the FRY and Serbia for the purpose of their expulsion. What is true in relation to this, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said several times that in my area the population left for the territory of the Republic of Albania through two border posts but primarily through Vrbnica. I cannot understand at all that the fact that I helped the Albanian population so that they would not sustain any losses in the minefields were considered to be escorting them, taking them out. With their own bodies my soldiers defended them. They protected them from getting into minefields because they would sustain losses that way. Or if I helped the elderly, women, and children who were standing by the road weak, exhausted, that that is considered to be use of vehicles for conducting ethnic cleansing. I did what I believe any normal person would do: I did not allow women and children to suffer, to stand by the road. Where I could, I gave medical assistance, I ordered that kind of assistance, or I made it possible for women, children, and old people to be transported to where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Paragraph 60 speaks of efforts of the forces of the FRY and Serbia to prevent the Albanians going back home by looting and robbing Kosovo Albanians of money and valuables, stealing personal vehicles and other property from Kosovo Albanians being deported from the province. Do you know about any of this since it was stated here that it was done by the forces of the FRY and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deported? That is a term which is certainly inappropriate. Today as well we went through documents related to individual cases of theft of vehicles or individual cases of appropriation of personal property. When something like that happened in my zone, I reacted the same moment, as soon as I heard of any such case. Since most of the inhabitants left through my zone, no one can show me a single inhabitant who got killed when entering my zone, any person who was leaving our state territory. I explained only one case of lack of discipline, leaving the column and coming across a mine. The entire population that entered my zone survived and left my zone healthy and alive. As for individual cases, I did not count them. I did not give any numbers, but there were reactions in response to each and every case. I said that documentation was mentioned. I myself was surprised when I saw this. According to my knowledge, that was only in that particular spot. At the other border post that is in my zone, that did not happen. I already said that border posts were not under my control. When I noticed that, I was with this TV crew from abroad because they wanted to go to the border. However, after having heard that and after having informed the head of the Secretariat of the Ministry of the Interior, this activity never occurred again. I think that this did not occur elsewhere either, especially refugees going to Montenegro or going to Macedonia, although I was not there myself. It all happened at this one particular place, and that was arbitrariness of individuals, of a group of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You just said that the borders were not under your control. Might it be, then, that the incidents did take place and you're not aware of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not only the border posts that are under my control. You know what the border actually is. That's only 50 metres along the state border. That is where the customs facilities are and the border police. So it's only that section that was not under my control. All the rest was under my control. One is Vrbnica, one is Cafa Pruse. Those were the two that were under my control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that with regard to this observation of yours you informed the chief of SUP. You talked about that yesterday. You said that he was surprised and that he stopped that.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I saw was very ugly. I was surprised myself, because quite simply I know that no such order existed and that what was done with these registration plates -- that's what I saw, I did not see the documents, that that is something very ugly, and I knew at the same moment that that was greatly harming our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, as an officer of the army of Yugoslavia throughout this time while you were there, while you were commander there, did you ever receive any orders to deport Kosovo Albanians from any part of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely never did I receive such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get a report or a plan about this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got orders from the corps command, some orders we saw yesterday, to find in my zone appropriate places where, if there was large-scale fighting, the population could be grouped and which zones would be safe in accordance with the rules and principles of the United Nations, that these zones should be marked and that I should inform the corps command about this, which areas in which villages in my zone I propose for putting up the civilian population so that it would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an officer, did you have any knowledge as to what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the ground myself all the time. My unit covered a zone of about 150 kilometres of the state border. My commanders were in their respective places. Every other day, my commanders reported except for the commander who was in the area of Djakovica who came only now and then. The rest came every other day to report and to be given their assignments. Every day they informed me about what happened in their zone or, rather, in the areas where they were, and about other events in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You had reports from your commanders. What about your superiors? Did they have daily information from you from the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had information every day, but as I've already said, people do not take a particular fact into account. You saw this video footage here. There is filming going on and aircraft are in the air all the time. For 78 days, day and night, all communications centres of the army were destroyed. All civilian communications centres were destroyed. There weren't even civilian communications in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. So my communication with my superior command was reduced to me sending a report in writing during the day, and by the time the command receives it, I mean all of its resources had also been hit, and I managed to speak to them very briefly through certain means of communication because they are very powerful and they are, therefore, registered immediately by the electronic surveillance aircraft of NATO. So there was communication. And precisely because there was a problem with communications, my superiors, the commander and Chief of Staff, who was otherwise in Djakovica, used each and every opportunity to come and visit my unit and to give me assignments directly. I can say that on average every fourth or fifth day the commander would come to my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Very briefly, what was the relationship between the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP like?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two state organs. Relations are correct and proper. They cooperate. They have their own scope of authority, we have our own scope. In 1998 and 1999, since this was the time of fighting terrorism, it so happened that some of our duty overlapped. I have a military police under my command, too, and also the Ministry of the Interior has some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authority over members of the military as well. I can assess that this cooperation was as it was supposed to be between state organs; professional and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What can you say about the Joint Command, which was referred to several times here? Was it within the chain of command or not? And who gave orders to you; the joint command or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the term "Joint Command," although as a matter of fact I received some orders, and I did not pay any attention to this term "Joint Command" because I usually received, on a regular basis, orders from my superior command of the Pristina Corps. Of course, this was on TV every day that a group of politicians, state officials from the republican and federal governments was in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that in Pristina there was a staff of the MUP for combatting terrorism. That's where the command of the Pristina Corps was as well. There was certainly meetings taking place between the two, but as for this group of politicians, they were there primarily to monitor the development of the political and security situation of Kosovo and Metohija, to cooperate with diplomatic, humanitarian and other organisations which were present on a daily basis, probably also to conduct certain talks and negotiations with the Albanians, to coordinate with the MUP and the army, and to express due interest in the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija. For me, the joint command -- I mean, I know that there was no joint command of any kind. My only commander was my commander, the commander of the Pristina Corps, and that was General Pavkovic in 1998. And in 1999 and during the war, it was General Lazarevic. So from time to time, very rarely, actually, I would receive orders from the Chief of Staff from the Pristina Corps. So those are the only two men who had the right to command me and to issue orders to me and it was only their orders that I would carry out. And of course, the commander of the army could order me something, or his Chief of Staff or somebody else from the chain of command. However, in practice that never actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mention is made here of a joint criminal enterprise. That's the term used, joint criminal enterprise. I'm sure you've heard it mentioned many times. Tell us now, please, General, briefly, what kind of enterprise did we have in Kosovo, undertaking?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo we had the fight against terrorism, against the terrorism that had support outside our country, and for that reason, that kind of terrorism was not able to be suppressed in the way in which it is usually suppressed and done in every other country, because in Kosovo we were fighting against terrorism. There was no -- the term "criminal enterprise" I don't know. I cannot accept that term because that would mean that I myself would have been in that criminal enterprise, involved in that criminal enterprise, and that in Kosovo and Metohija my area was very large, and I know what I did. I know full well what I did, I know full well what my unit did, what my men did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Finally, tell me this: I don't have a clear idea of all of this. From the office of Mr. Nice, did they call you to be an expert witness for Kosovo and Metohija, an expert for Kosovo and Metohija? You said you had a number of contacts with them, so how -- what did they say when they called you up?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. Nice's office. It was the office of the main Prosecutor, the Chief Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mrs. Carla Del Ponte, through her team located in Belgrade. So for two and a half years I worked on this intensively. I spent about 3.000 hours amassing documentation that the Prosecution had asked me for. Mr. Nice is trying to undermine in some way this kind of work, which I don't think is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have just one more question which I would like you to comment on. It is very specific and concrete. During the examination-in-chief, I received, as did you, this map. It was linked to the testimony of Ashdown, and it would appear that he was standing on the very border, the line of the very border, the frontier line between Yugoslavia and Albania, what can be seen from that point and so on. Now, as my associates, looking at it from that point which theoretically speaking is the most favourable position, although he says that he was by the village of Gegaj and not that particular point, he asked the Military Geographical Institute to mark this. So could you take a look at what we received from the Military Geographical Institute. It is on a scale of 1:50.000, the scale of the map, and we can have it placed on the overhead projector. So with your comments on that I will have completed my examination-in-chief. Would you be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Trial Chamber asked me to do, and as indeed Mr. Nice asked me to do, and as the subject I taught was topography, I did this for Mr. Nice in a short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one minute. I don't know what this map is. This is not the map that was handed by the witness to Ms. Dicklich. The map that was handed by the witness to Ms. Dicklich looks like this. It doesn't look to me to be the same unless I'm confused. So I don't know what this map is nor the writing on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what map have you handed to the witness? What map is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ELMO is exactly the same map. It is the identical map. Of course not Mr. Nice's, but I assume that geographical maps don't differ in any way. And my associates asked for the experts from the Military Geographical Institute mark down and shade in the areas that can be seen from the point that Mr. Nice marked on the map, which is the most favourable map, the vantage point, and it would appear as if he was standing at the very border, the frontier line, that is to say Ashdown, that he was at that point. And they did this very precisely at the Geographical Institute, Military Geographical Institute, more precisely than the witness could have done or could do now, so I just ask him to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that we can also see the map that I drew up, because I had a lot of problems. The map that I was provided with was of an unknown scale, so I had to determine the scale and I had no technical means to do this, technical equipment to help me to do that. But I did more or less the same thing that the experts from the institute did, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- institute is 155 years old. It's been in existence for that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking this question because the witness challenged Ashdown's testimony. So I just want him to tell us whether everything that Ashdown spoke about could actually be seen from the point he was at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map confirms that Mr. Ashdown could only have seen this first village, the first village that is found right up by the border watchtower of Morina and the valley there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you point to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if that's the point, if that's the point that Mr. Ashdown was standing at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's the most favourable point, let's assume, because that's on the very line of the actual border, the frontier line, although I doubt he was actually on that particular line but Mr. Nice took this as being the most favourable point.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did pursuant to requests from Mr. Nice is I moved this several hundred metres perhaps, the point -- I moved the point several hundred metres. But the map I was provided with, of course this map is far more precise. So from this point you can see -- here we have three or four kilometres and there is just one village that you can see from that point with the hamlets, the surrounding hamlets. I was there often. They are groups of houses in -- where certain households live. So that's the only village you can see. These other villages, Ponosevac and so on, cannot be seen. There are quite a number of valleys here and the shaded-in surfaces show that can be seen, these dark areas, and they are the slopes which, according to their altitude, are higher than the valleys. So the darkened-in areas is what you can see. The other areas are the valleys of the various streams that cannot be seen from that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, what stands in the way of their being seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, every point has its absolute height, as we call it, absolute altitude. So if in front of you you have -- if you're at a point and you have another point that is lower from the point where you are standing, it can be quite a lot lower, or if it is your same height, it prevents you from seeing everything that is behind that point, although you can have the feeling that what you can see is continuous. However, in your angle of vision you don't see the valleys and everything beyond these natural obstacles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since I am not a cartographer, show us on the map the points which are so high that they prevented him from seeing the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer your question briefly, what hampers seeing it? Nobody can see through a hill. Nobody can see through a mountain. That's the obstacle. So the darkened-in areas are the places that could be seen from the point. The areas in the valleys beyond those points cannot be seen. Here we have Skoza, which prevents you from seeing anything further in the distance along that way. Here we have another feature. This is a black and white copy so I can't read what it says, but it's a feature which, according to its altitude, is higher than this first point and limits vision. You cannot see further along that side. So this is your angle of vision. Under Ponosevac you have Planik. That's one feature there, Planik, and I know that from the map I drew up for Mr. Nice. It is at an altitude of 571 metres, I believe, I remember correctly. Everything below it is lower, so that area you cannot see up until this next feature, the next dark line, darkened-in area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you indicate the point where Junik is on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Junik, no, you can't see it at all here. It would be -- if this is Ponosevac, it would be in that general direction, in this general direction, but it is far beyond that next hill. So there's no possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see Morina on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you cannot see Morina. Morina is here. It is covered. You can't see it. Morina cannot be seen, Batusa cannot be seen, and after that you come to Junik. Junik is a village which is between -- situated between two hills, and you can only see Junik if you're right up on that adjacent hill above Junik, because it's in a gorge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you seen a film that was taken of the view he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean film?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the view was video recorded, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Different incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could I have a copy of this map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is to have a copy of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want me to show the map I drew up here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm sure Mr. Nice in his cross-examination will get to that. I don't want to waste time on it now. Thank you, General. I have no further questions for you. I have completed my examination-in-chief, Mr. Robinson. The opposite side is going to ask you some questions now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment, please. I apologise. Mr. Robinson, this video clip, the 21st, I assume that you understood my request to have that admitted into evidence, and tab 288 should contain one more document related to the KVM mission. It was omitted from my set of documents and from your set of documents by mistake. So I have that here. Tab 288 and 288A, which means the Serbian and English text. So I'd like to tender that into evidence and have it admitted as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is one of the things we don't understand that the accused is talking about. And the tab number for the Zjum near Prizren video is not clear to us either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The videos that I provided, we can check the numbers of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are trying to identify the tab number for the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nice, you are referring to 629, additional videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's what it is. Well, 629 is Albanians, Turks, and Romas, and that was digging in the trenches. 627 is said to be Osek-Hilj Djakovica, and neither of those would seem to be Zjum near Prizren, and therefore we don't have any detail, date, or anything like that to go on. We don't know what it is. It was played without being one of the itemised exhibits or indexed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 627, where mention is made of the village of Zjum, Prizren, from May 1999. It's near Djakovica. Tab 627.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It appears in B/C/S, not translated into English. Yes. Only the first part of that index was translated into English. You follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. We'll work on that basis. There's the rest of his exhibits to be dealt with. Rather than waste what limited time there is today, I don't know if that could be reviewed. My position would be we skipped so many documents in this file that anything that isn't skipped I'm not going to object to having been overruled in respect of the television programme but anything that has been skipped we needn't bother with. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you in the position to identify those tab numbers skipped?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not. I should have been doing it but I wasn't. I was tied up with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just raise one matter on that, on the skipping of documents? During the Prosecution case there was a witness called Karleusa who produced the investigation file concerning the lorry from Prizren that was found in the lake, and it's the corpses in the lorry. He produced investigation file full of statements by various people during his investigation of that matter, and the tabs were skipped. It was a collective, it spoke for itself, and the whole exhibit did go into evidence. So if sometimes there is a collective of materials by which looking at a few of those tabs is sufficient to describe the general nature, in my submission, that should not prevent the rest of the documents going on if they are part of that collective. The Trial Chamber may attach what weight to it they wish, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In this particular situation, we sanctioned the procedure whereby Mr. Milosevic dealt with a group of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So wouldn't it be reasonable to assume that if he didn't -- if he skipped something -- I'm not talking about the documents in the group. If there are documents in the group that were not specifically referred to, then those are admitted as part of the group. But if they're outside the group --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- it's reasonable to assume he wasn't seeking the admission of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have an issue with that. I was being careful about missed documents because there might be a misunderstanding between the parties on such an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you heard what I said to Mr. Kay, that we allowed you to deal with documents in groups. So if a group had ten documents and you only mentioned four, all of the ten will be admitted. But it's another question in relation to documents outside of the groups which were not -- which were not mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think in principle you are quite right, but in this specific case I didn't skip one single document. Let me remind you. I asked from you and from the witness to go through certain documents in groups, such as documents related to the KVM, and whenever I asked the witness to do so, I asked for your consent, such as in the case of reports for April and May. I asked that they be dealt with as a group with the witness highlighting only the main points, and with the proviso that all of them be admitted into evidence. We dealt with documents either by period or by type with your approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you saying you didn't skip any documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not if you bear in mind that I asked for your prior approval to go through certain documents by group as dealing specifically with only some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... deal with. You dealt with in the groups.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
